mutations.name: the PRIMARY loss returns: messages.js drops result.headers in the error translation, one step before the router
the PRIMARY loss returns on the Gemini side
the SECONDARY loss returns: the messages non-stream branch of the router stops forwarding result.headers
the SECONDARY loss returns on the Gemini route

SURVIVOR (documented): precedence inside withUpstreamHeaders is flipped so upstream headers would win over the translated response's own. Unobservable HERE because the two sides are disjoint in practice — toAnthropicError/geminiError set no `headers` key at all, so `response.headers` is undefined and either merge order yields the same object. Measured: suite stays 5/5 with the mutation applied. The ROUTE vocabulary (anthropic-version, request-id) is protected one layer up, in server.js, by the `!(k in anthropicHeaders)` test — and THAT is guarded, by the collision case in this file. Re-run this mutation if either error builder ever starts returning headers of its own; the order would then become observable and this would be the only guard.

SURVIVOR (documented): the empty/absent short-circuit is removed, so a translated error gains a `headers: {}` key it previously lacked. Harmless because every consumer reads it conditionally — server.js guards with `if (result.headers)` and an empty object is falsy-equivalent for its purposes (the for-loop body never runs), while the stream branch spreads it (spreading {} is a no-op). Measured: suite stays 5/5. The short-circuit is kept for identity, not behaviour: it lets a caller distinguish "not wrapped" from "wrapped, nothing to add", which matters when diffing responses in a test. Guarding it would mean asserting on the ABSENCE of a key, pinning an implementation detail rather than a behaviour.
